title: Dark mode as a real theme, not an invert
metaTitle: Dark mode as a checked theme
excerpt: A dark theme is a second set of surfaces and text colors you check on real screens. Invert the product and the borders and the shadows lie.
alt: A person in a purple shirt typing on a bright blue laptop at a round table. The lit screen fits a piece about checking a dark theme as its own set of colors.
caption: Check the pairs on the actual surface. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: Why is an invert filter not a dark theme?
faqs.answer: A filter flips every pixel, including photographs, logos, and shadows. Shadows become light stains, and borders stop meaning what they meant. A dark theme is a second set of colors for paper, ink, lines, and the accent, checked on real screens.

faqs.question: What contrast should dark theme text meet?
faqs.answer: WCAG 2.2 asks for at least 4.5 to 1 for normal text and 3 to 1 for large text. Interface parts that carry meaning, such as an input border or an icon, need about 3 to 1 against the adjacent color. Passing on a light background does not mean the same pair passes on dark paper.

faqs.question: How do you keep a dark theme from flashing on load?
faqs.answer: Paint the first HTML in the theme the person will actually get, using their saved choice or their system setting. A light page that flips to dark after the JavaScript loads feels broken and hides the content for a moment. Reload and watch the first frame before you call it done.

markdown:
A dark mode design system is a second set of surfaces and text colors that you check on real screens. It is not a filter. Invert the product and the borders and the shadows lie. Text that was dark on light becomes a glow, photographs turn into negatives, and the focus ring you tuned last month disappears.

Ship the dark theme as a set of tokens with the same jobs as the light ones. Paper, ink, a line, and one accent. Then look at both themes side by side before you call either of them done.

## A second palette, with the same jobs

Name the roles, not the hex values, in the conversation with the founder. Paper is the background the work sits on. Ink is the text. A line separates regions. One accent marks the action and the current selection. Each role gets a light value and a dark value. Components refer to the role. They do not refer to "gray-900" in one file and "white" in another.

The dark paper is rarely pure black, and the dark ink is rarely pure white. Slightly lifted paper and slightly softened ink reduce halation, the glow that makes white text on black feel like it is vibrating. You still have to measure contrast. Softening is a comfort. It is not an excuse to miss the standard.

The W3C's [WCAG 2 overview](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) points to WCAG 2.2 as the shared standard, with testable success criteria. The contrast minimum for normal text is 4.5 to 1. Large text can sit at 3 to 1. User interface components and graphical objects that carry meaning also need a 3 to 1 contrast against what is next to them. Those numbers apply to the dark theme on its own. A pair that passes on white paper can fail on dark paper even when you feel the colors are "the same brand."

Check the accent in both themes. A blue that is calm on white can fall under 4.5 to 1 when it becomes text on a navy surface, and it can become electric when you lighten it enough to pass. Adjust the accent's dark value on purpose. Write down the pair. If the founder cannot see them together, the next screen someone builds will invent a third blue.

## Why invert fails

A CSS filter that inverts colors is a demo. It flips every pixel, including the ones that were already correct.

Shadows are the obvious lie. A shadow on a light theme is a darker translucent shape under a card. Invert it and the shadow becomes a light stain, often in the wrong direction, as if the card were glowing from the table. On a dark theme, elevation is usually a lighter surface, a fine line, or both. It is not a black shadow sitting on black paper. Draw two or three elevations and stop. A product does not need eight depths.

Borders lie next. A border that was a dark line on white becomes, under invert, a light line that may or may not be visible, and it inverts again inside images and icons you did not mean to restyle. Give the line its own token. On dark paper the line is often a lighter translucent edge, checked against the 3 to 1 bar when it separates regions the user must tell apart. Decorative lines can be quieter. Functional ones cannot.

Photographs, logos, and product shots should not pass through the filter. A picture of a person, a shop, or a material has colors you do not own the right to flip. Mask those assets out of any theme trick, and choose them so they sit on both papers. A screenshot of the product used as marketing, with its own light UI, may need a frame or a separate crop for the dark page. Do not expect the filter to produce it.

Icons drawn as a single color can follow the ink token. Icons with several fills need a dark variant or a palette that already works on both papers. A logo with a wordmark in dark gray needs the version you already keep for dark backgrounds. Invert will give you a muddy substitute and call it a system.

## What you check, screen by screen

Make a list of surfaces and walk it in both themes. App background, card, popover, input, disabled, selected, danger, success. Each one has a background and a text color, and the text color has to pass on that background, not on the page in general.

Danger is where teams get hurt. A red chosen for white paper often fails as text on a dark red banner, and a pale red used as a background on white may become invisible on dark paper. Pick the danger pair in both themes. Do the same for success and warning. Status colors are a small system of their own. They are not the accent, reused until it means nothing.

Placeholders and disabled text are the other trap. They are allowed to be quieter, and they still have to be readable enough that a person can tell what the field wants. If the placeholder is the only label, it is not a placeholder. It is the label, and it owes the full contrast. Prefer a real label above the field in both themes.

Charts need their series checked, not inverted. A line that was dark blue on white may vanish on dark paper. Give each series a value per theme, and check that neighbors in the legend can be told apart without relying on color alone. A dot or a dash pattern carries the series when color is not enough.

Focus rings get the same pass. The ring that was ink-colored on light paper needs a light ring on dark paper, still offset, still 2 pixels or more. Select a control in both themes and look at it at arm's length. If you have to hunt, the ring is too polite.

## Preference, toggle, and the flash

Honor the system setting, and offer an in-product choice of light, dark, and match-the-system. Store the choice on the person, not only on the machine, if they use the product in more than one place. Say which one is in effect. A toggle that lies about the current theme will be clicked twice and then distrusted.

The first paint should match the theme they will get. A light page that flips to dark after hydration is a flash, and it is also a layout and trust problem. On a site built with server-rendered HTML, the theme can be known early enough to paint the right paper the first time, from a cookie or from the system setting inlined in a tiny script in the head. Pick one approach and test a reload. If you see a white frame before the dark one, you are not done.

Images that are the largest thing on a marketing page should be chosen for the theme around them, or given a background that works in both. A dark hero sitting on a light flash, then a dark page, feels broken even when the final frame is fine.

Reduced transparency and increased contrast, where the operating system offers them, are separate settings. You do not have to build a third brand. You do have to avoid making the dark theme depend on a translucent layer that disappears when transparency is reduced. Solid fallbacks for those surfaces belong in the token list.

## How the work stays small

Keep the token list short enough to print. If you have twenty grays in each theme, you do not have a system. You have a menu people will sample from at random. Four surfaces and two text levels, plus the line, the accent, and the status pairs, will cover a product a small team can actually maintain.

Document the pairs where designers and engineers both look. In Figma, the variables are the roles. In the code, the same role names appear in the Tailwind theme or the CSS variables. A dark value that exists only in a design file will drift the first time someone styles a new panel in the codebase. A dark value that exists only in code will drift the first time someone draws a new screen.

New components take both themes in the same pull request. A card that ships in light only is a bug, even if dark is "later." Later is how the invert filter sneaks back in as a temporary fix and stays.

Review with the lights in the room considered. A dark theme that only looks right in a dim office may be too dim for a founder working near a window. Step away from the monitor. If the ink sinks into the paper, lift the ink, then recheck the ratio. The number and the eye both have a vote. The number stops you from shipping a theme only you can see on a calibrated display.

## A review before you call it a theme

Put the light and dark screenshots in one file, the same layouts.

- Body text meets 4.5 to 1 in both.
- The line around an input is visible in both.
- Shadows are not inverted blurs. Elevation is a lighter surface or a drawn edge.
- Photos and logos are themselves, not filtered.
- Danger, success, and the focus ring each have a pair.
- Reload does not flash the other theme.

If any row fails, fix the token, not the one screen. Then look at a second screen and see if the token held.

Illustration is the next place a single unchecked color shows up. [Illustration systems for a product, not a poster](/blog/illustration-systems-for-a-product-not-a-poster) is the next piece: one line weight, one palette, one kind of scene, used to explain a step. An illustration painted for a light poster will sit badly on the dark paper you just specified, unless the palette was chosen with both in mind.

If you want a second pair of eyes on the tokens before they spread, book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). Bring the light screen and the dark one. The useful review is the pairs, side by side.
